video_title: The Bulls Are Back: Treasury Intervention, SEC Crypto Rules & Trump Says Hyperliquid
gist: Blockworks Research's Mark and Nick join host Luke to dissect a historic bullish week driven by three catalysts: a Treasury signal to buy back up to $1 trillion in 30-year bonds (reviving Bitcoin/gold as debasement hedges), the SEC's new 'Regulation Crypto Assets' capital-formation framework (favoring compliant issuers, onshore exchanges, mature DAOs, and ICOs over airdrop farming), and Trump publicly naming Hyperliquid as a CFTC onshoring target for perpetual futures. They also argue crypto's ETF-flow narrative has causality backwards (price drives flows, not vice versa) and lay out a base case for crypto closing 2026 higher despite likely near-term chop.

insights.claim: Treasury announced it will roughly double its monthly 30-year bond buybacks (from about $2B to $4B) and a subsequent media leak indicated it is considering buybacks of up to $1 trillion in 30-year Treasuries, though no purchases had actually been executed as of recording.
insights.speaker: host (Luke)
insights.so_what: Watch actual September purchase volumes against the trillion-dollar tease to gauge whether this is real yield-curve support or just forward guidance.
insights.quote: Sources say the Treasury is considering buying back up to a trillion uh in 30-year Treasury bonds.

insights.claim: The Treasury's buyback signaling functions as an implicit form of yield-curve control -- 'drawing a line in the sand' on how high long rates can go -- more than routine debt management, and this signal (not the buyback size) is what re-ignited Bitcoin and gold as debasement-trade assets.
insights.speaker: Mark (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Forward guidance, not delivered flow, is driving the debasement trade -- a retraction of the guidance, not just smaller buybacks, is the real risk to the thesis.
insights.quote: it's more like the Treasury drawing a line in the sand, saying that it's really uncomfortable with rates going higher

insights.claim: The 10-year Treasury yield sat around 4.70% and the 30-year around 5.20% (a roughly 50bp spread), while the 20-year was also pricing near 5.20% instead of the ~4.95% a normal curve interpolation implies -- an anomaly cited as the rationale for Treasury to buy back 20s while issuing more 10s and 30s.
insights.speaker: Mark (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: A persistently rich 20-year vs 30-year suggests further curve-shape trades (buy back the 20, issue more 10s/30s) rather than a change in total issuance size.

insights.claim: The buyback is explicitly not QE -- no new Treasuries are being printed, money is only reallocated within the Treasury's own balance sheet/cash management -- yet it appears to be producing a similar psychological 'not-QT' effect on risk assets as actual easing would.
insights.speaker: Mark (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: If markets are pricing this as easing when it's really just reallocation, the follow-through liquidity impact in coming months could disappoint relative to current enthusiasm.
insights.quote: it's not quantitative easing. We're not printing more money... it's just moving around treasuries and cash

insights.claim: Treasury buybacks in the $2-4B/month range are historically not unusual (precedent exists in prior years, especially around tax/cash-management periods) and are a 'drop in the bucket' against total US federal debt, which just crossed $40 trillion.
insights.speaker: Mark (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: The actual buyback size isn't the bullish catalyst -- the market is trading the forward-guidance signal that Treasury will act further if long yields keep rising.

themes.theme: AI Credit Boom Crowding Out Crypto

insights.claim: Over the trailing 12 months, more capital from private foreign investors flowed into US corporate bonds than into US Treasuries, with a large share of that corporate issuance coming from Mag-7-type companies raising debt to fund AI data-center buildouts.
insights.speaker: Mark (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: AI capex financing is now large enough to move the Treasury curve -- a slowdown in AI capex or credit demand could unexpectedly ease upward pressure on long yields.

insights.claim: The AI trade hurt crypto in two distinct ways: it diverted investor attention and speculative capital away from crypto, and it kept interest rates elevated longer by pulling capital into competing AI corporate bonds instead of Treasuries.
insights.speaker: Mark (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Crypto's rebound may be partly a function of AI-trade capital rotating or slowing -- AI capex/credit trends are a leading indicator worth tracking for crypto positioning.
insights.quote: AI hurt crypto more than most people think

insights.claim: The usual 'don't fight the Fed' crowding-out dynamic has been inverted -- AI corporate borrowers are now crowding out Treasury demand rather than the Fed crowding out other trades via rate policy.
insights.speaker: Mark (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Rate-sensitive trades now need to account for AI-driven corporate credit demand as a macro variable, not just Fed policy signals.

insights.claim: The SEC's proposed 'Regulation Crypto Assets' creates two exemptions plus one off-ramp: a $5M/6-month 'startup exemption' open to issuers globally; tiered 'fundraising exemptions' (tier 1 and tier 2) allowing up to $75M raised over 4 years but restricted to US-based issuers; and a Form TR certification path letting a token exit security/investment-contract status once deemed 'sufficiently functional,' also open to non-US issuers.
insights.speaker: Nick (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Issuers should map their raise size and domicile against these tiers now -- the $75M US-only tier will likely draw the bulk of new project filings.

insights.claim: Disclosure and audit obligations scale with raise size under Reg CA -- larger raises require not just disclosures but financial statements, and above a certain threshold those statements must be audited.
insights.speaker: Mark (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Projects planning $20M+ raises should budget for audited financials as a compliance cost of entry.

insights.claim: Under Reg CA, an 'investment contract' is defined per individual fundraising round or promise rather than across a project's entire lifetime (e.g., Uniswap v3 and v4 would each be separate investment contracts), which is expected to push teams toward raising capital more frequently in smaller, discrete rounds.
insights.speaker: Nick (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Expect a higher cadence of smaller, product-specific raises from established protocols rather than one-time mega-raises.

insights.claim: The regulation explicitly closes a 'no new promises' loophole -- a team cannot declare its original investment-contract promise fulfilled and then pivot to new development to escape disclosure obligations -- which could make protocols with genuinely functioning DAOs (broad external contributor participation) best positioned to credibly claim 'sufficiently functional' status.
insights.speaker: guest (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Mature, decentralized-governance DAOs could become a regulatory asset rather than a governance nuisance -- worth screening projects by real (not nominal) DAO activity.

insights.claim: The clearest beneficiaries of Reg CA are expected to be US-compliant issuers and onshore exchanges, since exchanges will be pushed to delist non-compliant tokens from US venues, causing a 'reckoning' in the CoinMarketCap/CoinGecko top-100 list, with early-compliant tokens receiving outsized new listings or avoiding delistings.
insights.speaker: Nick (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Screen top-100 tokens for compliance readiness -- laggards face US delisting risk while early compliant filers could see listing-driven demand.
insights.quote: you're going to see some tokens get delisted from US markets... early receive an outsized share of exchange listings

insights.claim: The SEC's Reg CA proposal is now in a 60-day public comment period before any rule or enforcement changes take effect.
insights.speaker: host (Luke)
insights.so_what: Watch which large industry players file comments or critiques during this window as a read on institutional sentiment toward the framework.

themes.theme: Clarity Act, Agency Turf & Regulatory Durability

insights.claim: Prediction-market odds of the Clarity Act passing fell to about 14% as of recording, after rallying to roughly 28% over the prior week.
insights.speaker: host (Luke)
insights.so_what: Clarity Act passage odds are a tradeable signal for crypto market-structure risk; a mid-September cloture vote is the next catalyst.

insights.claim: The Clarity Act has struggled to pass not primarily due to market-structure disagreements (its ostensible purpose) but because of unrelated sticking points -- ethics rules, money-laundering/illicit-finance provisions, and developer protections -- that weren't fully in scope of the original draft.
insights.speaker: Mark (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Even if Reg CA advances, Clarity-style comprehensive legislation may remain stuck on non-market-structure riders -- don't assume Reg CA substitutes for it.

insights.claim: Reg CA alone is not sufficient and further Congressional legislation will likely still be needed, but agency-level rulemaking (SEC, CFTC, FASB) is expected to serve as a durable stopgap because once many issuers have complied with new disclosure regimes, a change in presidential administration is unlikely to unwind that infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Mark (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Treat agency-level crypto disclosure rules as sticky, election-resilient policy rather than a fragile executive-branch initiative.
insights.quote: I don't see that just disappearing um just because an administration changes

insights.claim: Beyond the SEC, the CFTC has signaled it will pursue its own crypto-asset regulations and FASB has signaled similar action on stablecoins and cash-rebate/revival loans, suggesting multiple agencies are moving in parallel to fill the gap left by stalled comprehensive legislation.
insights.speaker: Mark (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Track CFTC and FASB rule proposals alongside SEC's Reg CA -- perpetuals/derivatives and stablecoin accounting rules could be the next regulatory catalysts.

insights.claim: Under Reg CA, if an airdrop requires any active participation or subsequent action from recipients after being announced -- including simple points-based farming -- that constitutes an 'exchange of consideration' making the airdrop an investment contract subject to exemption filing, and this is expected to push the ecosystem's token-distribution mix decisively toward ICOs over airdrops.
insights.speaker: guest (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Airdrop farming as currently practiced is now a regulatory target; position for renewed ICO deal flow and reduced airdrop-farming opportunity going forward.
insights.quote: if an airdrop requires any... specific or active participation... that would actually constitute... an exchange of consideration

insights.claim: Because Reg CA's sub-$5M startup exemption closely matches typical raise sizes on the Metadow ICO platform, the 'vibe coding' era -- where a single founder or tiny team can ship a product and raise capital around it -- is expected to accelerate, benefiting Metadow and the broader small-cap ICO pipeline.
insights.speaker: host (Luke)
insights.so_what: Metadow-style small-cap ICO volume is a bullish read-through of Reg CA; watch new raise counts on the platform post-ruling.

insights.claim: A guest pushes back on the Metadow bull case, arguing the past year has shown distribution and capital matter more than first-mover advantage in crypto -- a bank, exchange, or better-capitalized platform (citing Coinbase's acquisition of Echo as precedent) could replicate or out-compete Metadow's ICO launchpad.
insights.speaker: Nick (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Treat Metadow's ICO-launchpad lead as contestable rather than durable -- Coinbase/Echo-style consolidation is a real competitive risk.
insights.quote: distribution and capital matters a lot in the crypto space that more so maybe than first move advantage

insights.claim: ICOs are expected to become increasingly permissioned/KYC'd rather than fully permissionless as the sector re-emerges under Reg CA; Metadow is viewed as having built the most successful permissionless ICO launchpad so far (alongside a comparable EVM launchpad), but the model is expected to shift toward more first-time founders and differentiated raise structures.
insights.speaker: Nick (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Expect ICO platform economics to shift toward compliance/KYC infrastructure as a differentiator, not just permissionless access.

insights.claim: A trade-off exists between Metadow's programmatic-treasury model (fast, code-enforced refund/liquidation votes) and the new disclosure-heavy, audited-financial-statement regime -- a legal disclosure-based recourse process could take a year or two versus a programmatic treasury vote executable in about a month, suggesting programmatic structures retain a real speed advantage even as compliance requirements rise.
insights.speaker: Nick (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Programmatic treasury mechanisms may coexist with (not be replaced by) disclosure regimes as a complementary investor-protection feature.
insights.quote: if you can make this happen in a month instead of in a year, two years, it's it feels better

insights.claim: President Trump named Hyperliquid at a press conference attended by crypto industry leaders (including Brian Armstrong, Vlad Tenev, and Brad Garlinghouse), stating that CFTC Chairman Mike Selig is working to onshore the perpetual futures market including Hyperliquid; HYPE subsequently traded up more than 30% intraday to a new all-time high.
insights.speaker: host (Luke)
insights.so_what: A presidential-level mention plus a named CFTC onshoring effort is a concrete regulatory catalyst that materially re-rated HYPE -- watch for follow-through CFTC exemption filings.

insights.claim: Onshoring perpetuals would represent a step-function increase in Hyperliquid's total addressable market by opening access to the US retail and institutional investor base.
insights.speaker: host (Luke)
insights.so_what: An actual CFTC exemption for Hyperliquid would be a further re-rating catalyst beyond the current all-time-high reaction, not yet fully priced.

insights.claim: If Hyperliquid secures the regulatory exemption it needs, other consumer fintech apps (e.g., SoFi) are likely to integrate Hyperliquid's perpetuals rather than build proprietary perp products, positioning Hyperliquid to become both the default onshore perp infrastructure layer and the leading crypto-native perp exchange.
insights.speaker: Nick (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Hyperliquid's addressable market includes B2B2C infrastructure licensing to fintechs, not just direct retail volume -- a structural bull case beyond simple TAM expansion.
insights.quote: why would I build my own per product when I could just layer Hyperliquid on top of my app?

insights.claim: A live legal debate over whether perpetual futures are actually 'futures' or should be classified as 'swaps' (raised via a CME lawsuit argument, since perpetuals lack a delivery/expiration date but do exchange a funding rate) could materially affect the regulatory pathway and timing for onshoring, and the classification may differ by underlying asset -- Kalshi's already-approved short-dated Bitcoin perpetual-style products may not set precedent for equity-underlying perpetuals.
insights.speaker: Mark (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: The futures-vs-swap classification fight is an underappreciated risk/timing variable for onshored crypto perps -- a Bitcoin-underlying exemption may not translate cleanly to equity-underlying perps.

insights.claim: A proposed model from the Hyperliquid policy center would keep Hyperliquid as a neutral base layer with a permissioned compliance layer on top, with market makers sharing liquidity across permissioned and permissionless order books to preserve depth; if that liquidity instead fragments, competitors like Coinbase or Robinhood could offer competing perp products with superior order-book depth.
insights.speaker: Mark (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Whether Hyperliquid's liquidity stays unified across permissioned and permissionless venues is a key technical and competitive risk to monitor as onshoring proceeds.

insights.claim: Bitcoin posted the biggest one-week dollar-value candle in its history this week, with many long-tail altcoins rallying 100% or more over the same period.
insights.speaker: host (Luke)
insights.so_what: A record weekly move occurring right after 'beyond bleak' sentiment is being read as a likely cycle-low confirmation rather than a blow-off top.

insights.claim: Bitcoin ETF flows just posted their biggest weekly uptick in roughly 10 weeks, following large outflows in May and June and generally anemic demand through the summer, suggesting these vehicles may be setting a floor in AUM.
insights.speaker: host (Luke)
insights.so_what: A sustained reacceleration in ETF inflows, versus a one-week spike, is the key confirming signal to watch into year-end.

insights.claim: This week's Bitcoin short squeeze was the largest since 2021, but notably occurred without MicroStrategy/Michael Saylor actively adding to his position -- he was sidelined during the rally -- which is viewed as constructive because it shows demand is broader than one large concentrated buyer.
insights.speaker: host (Luke)
insights.so_what: Don't treat MicroStrategy's buying activity as a prerequisite for further upside -- broader, less concentrated demand appears to be emerging.
insights.quote: this rally happened without the support of his bid which I think is incredibly constructive

insights.claim: Digital-asset-treasury (DAT) company mNAVs are creeping back up toward 1.0x; if they turn positive, these companies are expected to resume tapping the ATM (at-the-market equity issuance) to buy more crypto, adding another source of buy-side flow.
insights.speaker: host (Luke)
insights.so_what: Watch DAT mNAVs crossing back above 1.0x as a leading indicator for renewed treasury-company buying pressure.

insights.claim: A Granger causality test between Bitcoin ETF flows and Bitcoin price found that price moves tend to cause ETF flows more than flows cause price, meaning the popular 'institutional ETF flows are driving the rally' narrative likely has the causality backwards.
insights.speaker: guest (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Reduce confidence in ETF-flow-led bull narratives; treat flow data as validation of price action rather than a leading indicator to trade off.
insights.quote: it's actually price that dictates what's going on... the more the price moves, the more the ETF flows happen

insights.claim: One guest's base case is that crypto closes 2026 above current levels, viewing the past week's euphoria as somewhat premature (expecting near-term chop or a modest pullback) but not close to a cycle top, with the next 3-6 months' trajectory hinging on retail sentiment follow-through and the substance of comments filed during the SEC's 60-day Reg CA comment period.
insights.speaker: Nick (Blockworks Research)
insights.so_what: Use the Reg CA comment-period disclosures as a read on institutional conviction before adding further risk.

insights.claim: Another guest, who previously published 'bottom signals' work, says the rally already fulfilled his modeled bull case sooner and more forcefully than expected; he now expects possible sideways consolidation for a few weeks and wants to see a higher low form on a high-timeframe uptrend before targeting materially higher prices through 2027-2028.
insights.speaker: host (Luke)
insights.so_what: A higher-low confirmation after this week's spike, rather than immediate further upside, is the technical setup to watch before adding risk into year-end.
